title: Elbow examination: lateral elbow pain

guidelineVersions: BESS patient care pathway: tennis elbow (Shoulder Elbow, 2023)

related.why: C6 radiculopathy can refer pain to the lateral elbow
Same look, feel, move structure; screen the joint above
Ulnar nerve signs in the hand

brief.scenario: Mr Dominic Kessell, 46, a right-handed plasterer, has had pain on the outer side of his right elbow for four months. It is worse when he grips a trowel or lifts a bucket. There was no injury.
brief.task: Examine his elbows. You will be stopped at 6 minutes to present your findings and answer questions.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Look front, side and back; feel the bony points; move; provoke; then the ulnar and radial nerves, neck and shoulder.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Stopping at a tender epicondyle and missing a nerve cause or referred pain from the neck.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Could you show me where it hurts with one finger?"

flow: Feel: bony points and ulnar nerve

grid.label: Preparation and exposure
grid.fail: Examines one elbow through a sleeve.
grid.pass: Introduces, confirms identity, gains consent, asks about pain, and exposes both arms to the shoulders.
grid.high: Asks him to point to the pain with one finger and compares with the other elbow throughout.

grid.label: Look
grid.fail: Inspects the front of the elbow only.
grid.pass: Inspects front, side and back with arms extended: carrying angle, swelling, olecranon bursa, scars, and wasting of the hand muscles.
grid.high: Names cubitus valgus or varus from an old fracture, and checks the hand for ulnar clawing.

grid.label: Feel
grid.fail: Doesn't find the point of maximal tenderness.
grid.pass: Palpates the lateral and medial epicondyles, the radial head while rotating the forearm, the olecranon, and the ulnar nerve in its groove.
grid.high: Checks for tenderness just distal to the epicondyle over supinator, which suggests radial tunnel syndrome instead.

grid.label: Move
grid.fail: Tests flexion only, or leaves out rotation.
grid.pass: Active and passive flexion and extension, then pronation and supination with elbows tucked in; compares sides.
grid.high: Says a full, painless range makes joint pathology unlikely, and screens the neck and shoulder for referred pain.

grid.label: Provocation tests
grid.fail: Uses no provocation test, or can't describe one.
grid.pass: Resisted wrist extension (Cozen's) or passive wrist flexion with the elbow straight (Mill's) reproduces lateral epicondyle pain.
grid.high: Adds resisted middle finger extension (Maudsley's) and notes pain-free grip strength as a baseline.

grid.label: Nerves and circulation
grid.pass: Tests little finger sensation, finger abduction, Froment's sign and Tinel's sign over the cubital tunnel; checks finger extension and the radial pulse.
grid.high: Adds the elbow flexion test for cubital tunnel syndrome, and explains weak finger extension would suggest posterior interosseous nerve compression.

grid.label: Presentation at the signal
grid.pass: Presents right lateral elbow tendinopathy: tender lateral epicondyle, positive provocation tests, full range, no neurological deficit.
grid.high: Leads with the diagnosis, then the negatives that exclude radial tunnel syndrome, C6 radiculopathy and joint pathology.

grid.label: Management
grid.fail: Offers a steroid injection as first-line treatment.
grid.pass: Explains it is usually self-limiting; offers physiotherapy with loading exercises and short-term topical NSAIDs; no routine imaging.
grid.high: States steroid injection helps briefly but gives worse results at a year, so BESS advises against it; 89% improve within a year.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Roll up your right sleeve, please. [Examines one arm through the sleeve.]

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: [Presses around the elbow.] It's sore somewhere here. Bend it for me. [Flexion only.]

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: [No provocation tests.] I'll leave the nerves, he's got no pins and needles.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: He has a painful right elbow.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello, I'm Dr Patel, one of the surgical trainees. Can I check your name and date of birth? I'd like to examine both your elbows. Is it sore now? Could you take your top off? [Cleans hands.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Arms out, palms forward; looks front, side and back.] Normal carrying angle, no swelling, no bursa, no scars, no wasting.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Palpates both epicondyles, radial head while rotating, olecranon, ulnar nerve.] Tender over the right lateral epicondyle.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Flexion, extension; pronation and supination with elbows tucked in.] Full range both sides.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Push your wrist up against my hand. [Pain at the lateral epicondyle.] Now I'll bend your wrist down with the elbow straight. [Pain.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Little finger sensation, finger abduction, Froment's, Tinel's at the cubital tunnel, finger extension, radial pulse.] Normal.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Mr Kessell has right lateral elbow tendinopathy: tender lateral epicondyle, pain on resisted wrist extension and passive stretch, full range, and no neurological deficit.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: It usually settles. I'd refer him for physiotherapy with loading exercises, advise modifying his grip, and suggest a topical NSAID for a few weeks. He doesn't need imaging.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello, I'm Dr Patel. Can I check your name and date of birth? Could you point to the pain with one finger? [Lateral epicondyle.] I'll compare with your left elbow as I go.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Front, side, back.] Normal carrying angle, no cubitus valgus or varus, and no clawing or wasting in the hands.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Palpates.] Tender at the lateral epicondyle, not distal to it over supinator, so radial tunnel syndrome is less likely.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Full range.] A full, painless range makes joint pathology unlikely. [Screens neck and shoulder: normal.]

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Cozen's and Mill's positive.] Straighten your middle finger against me. [Maudsley's positive.] Grip strength is reduced by pain.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Ulnar nerve tests; elbow flexion test negative.] Finger extension is strong, so no posterior interosseous nerve compression.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Right lateral elbow tendinopathy. The negatives: no tenderness over supinator, a normal neck and full elbow movement, so I don't think this is radial tunnel syndrome, C6 radiculopathy or joint pathology.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: A steroid injection helps for a few weeks but the results at a year are worse than placebo, so BESS advises against it. I'd explain that 89% improve within a year, and offer physiotherapy with loading exercises and a short course of topical NSAID.

failures.move: Leaving out the ulnar nerve and finger extension.
failures.consequence: Misses cubital tunnel syndrome or posterior interosseous nerve compression.

failures.move: Not screening the neck and shoulder.
failures.consequence: Referred pain from a C6 radiculopathy is misdiagnosed as tennis elbow.
Short-term relief but worse outcome and more recurrence at a year.

failures.move: Looking only at the front of the elbow.
failures.consequence: Misses an olecranon bursa and the carrying angle.

recovery.line: Before I finish, I'd like to test the ulnar nerve and finger extension, because nerve compression can mimic this.
It gives short-term relief, but outcomes at a year are worse, so I'd start with physiotherapy.

knowledge.fact: Lateral elbow tendinopathy is diagnosed clinically; Cozen's, Mill's and Maudsley's tests support it. Imaging only if the diagnosis is uncertain.
BESS: physiotherapy (strong for); corticosteroid injection (strong against); topical or oral NSAIDs for up to 4 weeks.
Steroid injection versus placebo: less recovery and more recurrence at one year.
Ulnar nerve: little finger sensation, interossei, Froment's sign, Tinel's at the cubital tunnel.
Olecranon bursitis: septic and aseptic overlap clinically; aspirate for Gram stain, culture and crystals.

recall.think: Is this really the tendon, or a nerve, the neck, or the joint?
recall.say: "Right lateral elbow tendinopathy, with no neurological deficit."
do: Look front, side, back; feel bony points
Ulnar and radial nerves; neck and shoulder

numbers.meaning: improve within a year without active treatment

recall.trap: A tender epicondyle doesn't exclude a nerve or neck cause.
recall.finish: Explanation, physiotherapy with loading, short-term topical NSAID; avoid steroid injection.

sources.name: ICBSE Guide to the intercollegiate MRCS examination
sources.supports: Introduce yourself, confirm identity, obtain consent and clean hands at every station; 6-minute signal in examination stations

sources.name: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery (O'Connell, McCaskie, Sayers, eds)
sources.supports: Elbow examination (look, feel, move); carrying angle, cubitus valgus and varus; ulnar nerve examination (Froment's sign, interossei, Tinel's sign, elbow flexion test); radial tunnel syndrome and posterior interosseous nerve compression; radial head fracture and fat pad sign

sources.name: Singh HP, Watts AC, et al., on behalf of the BESS LET Guideline Development Group. BESS patient care pathway: Tennis elbow. Shoulder Elbow 2023;15(4):348–359
sources.supports: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by Cozen's, Mill's or Maudsley's tests; radiographs not essential; imaging only where there is diagnostic uncertainty; physiotherapy recommended (strong); corticosteroid injection should not be used (strong); topical or oral NSAIDs for short-term relief up to 4 weeks; in a meta-analysis of untreated patients, 89% had global improvement in the first year; elbow red flags (injury, swelling or lumps, inflammation of several joints, suspected malignancy) need secondary care referral

sources.name: Coombes BK, Bisset L, Brooks P, Khan A, Vicenzino B. Effect of corticosteroid injection, physiotherapy, or both on clinical outcomes in patients with unilateral lateral epicondylalgia: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA 2013;309(5):461–9
sources.supports: Corticosteroid injection gave lower complete recovery or much improvement at 1 year than placebo (83% vs 96%) and greater 1-year recurrence (54% vs 12%)

sources.name: Reilly D, Kamineni S. Olecranon bursitis. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2016;25(1):158–67
sources.supports: Septic and aseptic olecranon bursitis overlap in clinical and laboratory findings; tenderness, erythema, warmth and fever are more frequent in septic bursitis; aspiration for diagnosis

partner.opening: Please examine this gentleman's elbows. I'll stop you at 6 minutes.
partner.actorBrief: You are Mr Dominic Kessell, 46, a right-handed plasterer. Four months of pain on the outer side of your right elbow, worse gripping a trowel or lifting a bucket. No injury, no neck pain, no pins and needles, no swelling. Point to the bony bump on the outside of the elbow. Wince when the doctor presses there or tests wrist extension against resistance. You have heard injections work and would like one.

reveals.finding: Normal, symmetrical carrying angle. No swelling, bursa, scars or muscle wasting.

reveals.trigger: Palpates the bony landmarks and ulnar nerve
reveals.finding: Tender over the right lateral epicondyle only. Not tender over supinator, radial head, olecranon or medial epicondyle. Ulnar nerve not tender and doesn't sublux.

reveals.trigger: Tests movements; screens neck and shoulder
reveals.finding: Full, painless flexion, extension, pronation and supination. Neck and shoulder normal.

reveals.trigger: Performs Cozen's, Mill's or Maudsley's test
reveals.finding: All reproduce pain at the right lateral epicondyle. Grip reduced by pain.
Normal sensation; finger abduction, finger extension and Froment's normal; Tinel's and elbow flexion test negative; radial pulse normal.
Say: "Please stop there and present your findings."

push.question: How would you tell this from radial tunnel syndrome?
push.expect: Radial tunnel: tenderness distal to the epicondyle over supinator; pain on resisted supination.

push.question: How do you examine the ulnar nerve at the elbow?
push.expect: Little finger sensation, finger abduction, Froment's sign, Tinel's at the cubital tunnel, elbow flexion test.

push.question: Would you image him?
push.expect: No; imaging only if the diagnosis is uncertain.

curveballs.prompt: The back of his elbow is swollen, hot and red, with a graze over it.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Possible septic olecranon bursitis: aspirate for Gram stain, culture and crystals before antibiotics.

curveballs.prompt: His little finger is numb and his pinch grip is weak.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Ulnar neuropathy at the cubital tunnel: examine fully and request nerve conduction studies.

curveballs.prompt: A different patient fell on her outstretched hand and can't fully straighten her elbow.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Examine neurovascular status; X-ray looking for a radial head fracture or a raised fat pad.

curveballs.prompt: He insists on a steroid injection.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Explain short-term relief but worse outcomes at a year; BESS advises against it; offer physiotherapy.
